# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- executable-requirements / ui_testing: How are the executable UI requirements exercised — what is the UI-testing mechanism (browser/E2E such as Playwright, DOM-level golden rendering, a headless harness), or is there none yet? Most requirements should be verifiable by a short test that drives to a state and makes a VISUAL assertion (a committed golden the owner checks by sight), so this fixes how a requirement becomes that assertion. [distill: recorded as intent; it fixes the harness the requirements.md drives its UI gates through, and the visual-golden path most leaves take for simplest owner verification]
- executable-requirements / requirements_source: Where do the requirements come from — an existing requirements/spec document, the issue tracker, or authored fresh? Name the path or source so the spec is seeded from it rather than reinvented. [distill: record the source; set config.spec to the executable spec's home (default dev/requirements/requirements.md) and extract the initial requirements from the named source]
- product-wiki / product: What is the product — what does it do, and what is the core value it delivers? If the repo already carries a product brief or spec, read it and confirm rather than asking cold. [distill: recorded as intent on this entry (the pack takes no config); it names what the research is about and frames every seeded wiki]
- product-wiki / users: Who are the users or customers — the segments whose needs the research must track? [distill: recorded as intent; scopes the user-research wiki and whose problems the findings answer to]
- product-wiki / market: What market or category is this in, and who are the main competitors or alternatives? This is what the competitor research is scoped against. [distill: recorded as intent; names the competitor set the initial competitor-landscape wiki is seeded from]

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- chrome-store-releases: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-and-ci: Drive this repo's PR-to-merged flow cheaply — when to open the PR, how to get CI green in a Claude web session, how to poll without wasting wall time or tokens, and when to arm auto-merge instead of waiting. Use whenever a session opens, watches, or lands a PR here — including one opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended or scheduled run, and any moment you ask "is CI green yet?" — not only for a deliberate merge or an e2e/heavy/UI change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- snapshot-approval: Get owner approval for a moved UI-snapshot baseline. Use whenever a change to a dev/requirements case (its spec or its rendering) makes the snapshot tests fail — the pixels moved and the baseline wants to change.
- testing-guide: Map of this repo's test suites, the requirements model, and where each harness documents itself. Use before writing or changing tests here, adding a requirement case, or debugging a suite — the invariants live in the gcec pack's RULES.md; this is the deeper how-to.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). # Rule revalidation — re-probe the claims whose truth lives outside this repo

Most of a pack's prose is judgment: how to approach a change, what to do first, what never to do. Judgment does not expire. A smaller set of rules is different — each one asserts a **fact about the environment**: that the harness accepts a call in a certain shape, that the Action's token can or cannot reach a path, that an MCP tool exists, that a platform behaves a particular way. Those were true on the day they were written and are true today only by luck, because nothing in this repo turns red when a platform moves under them. The prose stays green, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost arrives as a session spent on a route that closed.

This task re-runs the probe behind each such claim, weekly, and corrects what no longer holds.

The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to revalidate and the two probe rules below. Work those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. A canon pack a repo only mounts is revalidated in the repo that owns it, on this same task.

Open a PR and leave it for review. This task rewrites the rules sessions obey, on evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive from the diff, so every run's changes go in front of the owner.

## What counts as a revalidatable claim

A sentence in a rule, a check's `failureMessage` or `fix` text, or a skill's procedure, that would be **falsified by a change nobody in this repo makes**. The three richest seams:

- **The Claude environment** — tool contracts and their failure modes (what `Edit` requires before it will apply, what a scheduling call rejects, what a search returns for a bare name), which harness surfaces exist, what a session can and cannot see.
- **GitHub permissions and API behaviour** — what the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may push or label, what a path refuses, which status a call returns, what a repository setting gates.
- **MCP functions** — that a named tool exists, what its parameters are called, what it returns, which server carries it.

Also fair game: any rule naming a version floor, a runtime's behaviour, or an external service's response shape.

**Not** in scope, and left alone without a probe: judgment and taste rules; rules about how *this* repo is organized (a check already guards those, and a stale one fails loudly); product requirements; anything whose truth a reviewer could settle by reading the tree.

## The probe

A claim is revalidated by **executing the smallest thing that would distinguish true from false**, and reporting what actually happened — never by recalling what you know, and never by reasoning from the rule's own wording.

Two rules bound it, both binding scope from the dispatch:

1. **Read-only.** Probe by doing the harmless half: call the tool and read its schema, request the resource, run the command that reports rather than acts. A claim whose probe would **write, delete, merge, publish, notify, or spend a credential** is not probed — verify it against authoritative documentation and say in the log that documentation, not a run, is the evidence.
2. **A probe you cannot run is `unprobed`, not disproven.** This session carries the reach its repo was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under. A tool that is absent *here*, a permission denied *to this session*, a network path the sandbox blocks — none of that is evidence the claim is stale. Leave the rule exactly as it stands, log it as unprobed, and move on. Rewriting a rule into "you cannot do X" because *this* session could not is the single worst outcome available to this task: it is unfalsifiable afterwards, and it removes a capability from every future session.

## What a run does

1. **Enumerate.** Read the Context's pack paths and list **every** revalidatable claim in them, by the test above. Most of a pack is judgment prose and out of scope, so this set is far smaller than the corpus — and taking all of it every run is what lets this task hold no state between runs: there is nothing to remember about what a previous run covered. Order the work by what staleness would cost — a rule that would send a session down a dead path before a version number in a comment — so a run that runs out of budget has spent it on the claims that mattered, and says in its PR body which claims it did not reach.
2. **Probe each**, per the rules above, and record what you ran and what came back.
3. **Correct what is stale**, as far as the probe reaches and no further — one probe answers one claim, and a neighbouring claim it seems to imply gets its own probe. Rewrite the rule to what the probe showed, in the same voice and at the same length, and carry the *new* fact — not a note about the correction, and not a dated changelog. Where the claim was a check's premise rather than prose, and the check itself is now asserting a dead fact, fix the check and its fixture. Where a claim has become simply irrelevant (the surface it describes is gone), delete the rule whole rather than trimming it toward nothing.
4. **Open a PR** — one per run, on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. The PR body is the evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive: per changed rule, the probe run and its result. Keep the repo's offline test suite green.
5. **Report every verdict in the PR body**, and record the corrections in the pack. The PR body carries the full list — every claim probed with its verdict, `holds`, `stale (corrected)`, `unprobed (why)` or `doc-verified`, and the probe behind each — because a reviewer cannot re-derive any of it from the diff, and an `unprobed` claim needs naming as loudly as a corrected one. Each rule actually **corrected or deleted** also gets a row at the top of its pack's `VERSIONS.md` table, in the same commit: date, `rule-revalidation`, what the probe showed. `holds` and `unprobed` change nothing, so they leave no row — the file records what happened to the pack, not that a run happened. There is no standing issue.

A run that found everything still true opens no PR at all, and says so in its run log.

10	// prose-to-checks-sweep reads, so a repo names its capture surface once: a
11	// consuming repo revalidates only its OWN local packs, and Claudinite (which

15	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
16	
17	// The repo's own capture surface — a consumer revalidates only its LOCAL packs.
18	const DEFAULT_PACK_PATHS = ['.claudinite/local/packs'];
19	
20	export default {
21	  id: 'rule-revalidation',
22	  frequency: 'weekly',             // the environment moves on a platform's clock, not this repo's — see the cadence note
23	  precondition_signals: [],              // nothing in the repo signals that the world changed; the trigger is the calendar
24	  agent_model: 'opus',                   // designing a safe probe per claim, and reading a null result correctly, is heavy judgment
25	  expected_outcome: 'open-pr',           // it rewrites rules sessions obey — reviewed, never auto-merged
26	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
27	  agent_execution_timeout: 2700,         // reading the corpus + running real probes — a generous bound
28

30	  // repo to move; this one exists precisely because the repo does NOT move when
31	  // its claims expire — the harness ships, a token's scope narrows, an MCP server
32	  // drops a tool, and the only local evidence is a session failing later. So the
33	  // calendar is the whole trigger, and the slice-per-run discipline in task.md is
34	  // what keeps a standing corpus affordable.
35	  precondition(_signals, config) {
36	    const paths = Array.isArray(config?.pack_paths) && config.pack_paths.length ? config.pack_paths : DEFAULT_PACK_PATHS;
37	    return {
38	      run: true,
39	      reason: `weekly revalidation of environment-dependent claims in ${paths.join(', ')} (no-ops cheaply when every probe still passes)`,
40	      context: [
41	        `Pack paths to revalidate (these, and only these): ${paths.join(', ')}.`,
42	        'Probe read-only. A claim whose probe would write, delete, merge, publish, or notify is verified from authoritative documentation instead — never by performing it.',

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- chrome-store-releases: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-and-ci: Drive this repo's PR-to-merged flow cheaply — when to open the PR, how to get CI green in a Claude web session, how to poll without wasting wall time or tokens, and when to arm auto-merge instead of waiting. Use whenever a session opens, watches, or lands a PR here — including one opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended or scheduled run, and any moment you ask "is CI green yet?" — not only for a deliberate merge or an e2e/heavy/UI change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- snapshot-approval: Get owner approval for a moved UI-snapshot baseline. Use whenever a change to a dev/requirements case (its spec or its rendering) makes the snapshot tests fail — the pixels moved and the baseline wants to change.
- testing-guide: Map of this repo's test suites, the requirements model, and where each harness documents itself. Use before writing or changing tests here, adding a requirement case, or debugging a suite — the invariants live in the gcec pack's RULES.md; this is the deeper how-to.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.

This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.

1	# Rule revalidation — re-probe the claims whose truth lives outside this repo
2	
3	Most of a pack's prose is judgment: how to approach a change, what to do first, what never to do. Judgment does not expire. A smaller set of rules is different — each one asserts a **fact about the environment**: that the harness accepts a call in a certain shape, that the Action's token can or cannot reach a path, that an MCP tool exists, that a platform behaves a particular way. Those were true on the day they were written and are true today only by luck, because nothing in this repo turns red when a platform moves under them. The prose stays green, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost arrives as a session spent on a route that closed.
4	
5	This task re-runs the probe behind each such claim, weekly, and corrects what no longer holds.
6	
7	The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to revalidate and the two probe rules below. Work those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. A canon pack a repo only mounts is revalidated in the repo that owns it, on this same task.
8	
9	Open a PR and leave it for review. This task rewrites the rules sessions obey, on evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive from the diff, so every run's changes go in front of the owner.
10	
11	## What counts as a revalidatable claim
12	
13	A sentence in a rule, a check's `failureMessage` or `fix` text, or a skill's procedure, that would be **falsified by a change nobody in this repo makes**. The three richest seams:
14	
15	- **The Claude environment** — tool contracts and their failure modes (what `Edit` requires before it will apply, what a scheduling call rejects, what a search returns for a bare name), which harness surfaces exist, what a session can and cannot see.
16	- **GitHub permissions and API behaviour** — what the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may push or label, what a path refuses, which status a call returns, what a repository setting gates.
17	- **MCP functions** — that a named tool exists, what its parameters are called, what it returns, which server carries it.
18	
19	Also fair game: any rule naming a version floor, a runtime's behaviour, or an external service's response shape.
20	
21	**Not** in scope, and left alone without a probe: judgment and taste rules; rules about how *this* repo is organized (a check already guards those, and a stale one fails loudly); product requirements; anything whose truth a reviewer could settle by reading the tree.
22	
23	## The probe
24	
25	A claim is revalidated by **executing the smallest thing that would distinguish true from false**, and reporting what actually happened — never by recalling what you know, and never by reasoning from the rule's own wording.
26	
27	Two rules bound it, both binding scope from the dispatch:
28	
29	1. **Read-only.** Probe by doing the harmless half: call the tool and read its schema, request the resource, run the command that reports rather than acts. A claim whose probe would **write, delete, merge, publish, notify, or spend a credential** is not probed — verify it against authoritative documentation and say in the log that documentation, not a run, is the evidence.
30	2. **A probe you cannot run is `unprobed`, not disproven.** This session carries the reach its repo was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under. A tool that is absent *here*, a permission denied *to this session*, a network path the sandbox blocks — none of that is evidence the claim is stale. Leave the rule exactly as it stands, log it as unprobed, and move on. Rewriting a rule into "you cannot do X" because *this* session could not is the single worst outcome available to this task: it is unfalsifiable afterwards, and it removes a capability from every future session.
31	
32	## What a run does
33	
34	1. **Enumerate.** Read the Context's pack paths and list **every** revalidatable claim in them, by the test above. Most of a pack is judgment prose and out of scope, so this set is far smaller than the corpus — and taking all of it every run is what lets this task hold no state between runs: there is nothing to remember about what a previous run covered. Order the work by what staleness would cost — a rule that would send a session down a dead path before a version number in a comment — so a run that runs out of budget has spent it on the claims that mattered, and says in its PR body which claims it did not reach.
35	2. **Probe each**, per the rules above, and record what you ran and what came back.
36	3. **Correct what is stale**, as far as the probe reaches and no further — one probe answers one claim, and a neighbouring claim it seems to imply gets its own probe. Rewrite the rule to what the probe showed, in the same voice and at the same length, and carry the *new* fact — not a note about the correction, and not a dated changelog. Where the claim was a check's premise rather than prose, and the check itself is now asserting a dead fact, fix the check and its fixture. Where a claim has become simply irrelevant (the surface it describes is gone), delete the rule whole rather than trimming it toward nothing.
37	4. **Open a PR** — one per run, on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. The PR body is the evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive: per changed rule, the probe run and its result. Keep the repo's offline test suite green.
38	5. **Report every verdict in the PR body**, and record the corrections in the pack. The PR body carries the full list — every claim probed with its verdict, `holds`, `stale (corrected)`, `unprobed (why)` or `doc-verified`, and the probe behind each — because a reviewer cannot re-derive any of it from the diff, and an `unprobed` claim needs naming as loudly as a corrected one. Each rule actually **corrected or deleted** also gets a row at the top of its pack's `VERSIONS.md` table, in the same commit: date, `rule-revalidation`, what the probe showed. `holds` and `unprobed` change nothing, so they leave no row — the file records what happened to the pack, not that a run happened. There is no standing issue.
39	
40	A run that found everything still true opens no PR at all, and says so in its run log.
41

1 # gcec rules 2 3 The project's standing working rules — injected at session start while this pack 4 is declared. Activity-scoped procedures live in this pack's skills 5 (snapshot-approval, merge-and-ci, testing-guide) and surface on 6 demand; the extractor-automation domain's standing rules are the "Extractor 7 pipeline" section below, and its scheduled tasks live under `tasks/`. 8 9 ## Working rules 10 11 - **Never carry uncommitted edits onto a new branch with 12 `git checkout -- `** — that restores the paths' *committed* 13 content, silently destroying exactly the edits it was meant to preserve. 14 `git checkout -b origin/main` already brings a clean working tree along; 15 when it can't, commit or `git stash` first and never in the same `&&` chain 16 that moves the branch. In #734 the combined one-liner wiped three finished 17 edits **and** invalidated the `check_the_world.mjs` + `npm run test:offline` 18 pass that had just gone green, forcing a full re-verification. 19 - **A duplicate dispatch-trigger arriving while a session's own delegated 20 subagent is still running is a signal to stop, not to investigate.** 21 Confirm it via `resolve-dispatch` (the "not mine, change nothing" case) and 22 end the turn — don't let that check snowball into re-reading the subagent's 23 targets and redoing its work. In #876 a dispatched `tidy-issues` subagent 24 was still running in the background when a duplicate webhook fired; the 25 top-level session's "just confirming" pass over all 16 target issues 26 escalated into closing one and posting reconfirmation comments on the 27 rest — duplicating, not verifying, work its own subagent was already 28 producing — and converged the dispatch issue on that duplicate instead of 29 the subagent's actual output. 30 - **Cap and qualify every GitHub MCP list/search call** — an unbounded one 31 hard-fails the tool-result cap and costs a 2–3-call dig through the saved 32 result file. `search_issues` handed a bare title string full-text-searches the 33 whole repo and returns every match with its full body: the standing 34 `Claudinite tracker: ` lookup that opens every scheduled task blew up at 35 185–211 KB three times (#734 twice, #753), and `actions_list` without a page 36 cap at 155 KB (#760). Qualify the query (`in:title "Claudinite tracker: 37 "`, or `list_issues` + `labels`) **and** pass a small `perPage` (5–10) — 38 the answer wanted is one issue or one run, never a page of them. `perPage` 39 alone isn't the whole fix: even a single matched issue's full body can be 40 100+ KB, so the same overflow recurred with `in:title` correctly set but 41 `perPage` left off (#879, #890, #896). Pass `fields` too (e.g. `['number', 42 'title', 'state']`) to strip the body outright — a query that added it 43 (#886) returned instantly at ~3 KB where the identical unfielded query the 44 day before (#879) overflowed at 113 KB. 45 - **This repo's one divergence from the canon merge recipe: CI must be green 46 first** — twice for e2e/heavy-browser changes. The project mechanics of driving 47 a merge (dispatching CI in a web session, the poll back-off, when to arm 48 auto-merge instead of waiting) are the merge-and-ci skill — **load it for any PR a session opens**, including one 49 opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended run, not only for a deliberate 50 merge. 51 - **`npm run regen` is the regenerator** (load lists + UI snapshots + 52 generic-coverage baseline/report); a stale artifact can't slip through — its 53 own gate fails. On the `ours` driver (kept in sync with `.gitattributes`): 54 `extension/event-extractors/load-order.generated.json` (from `npm run index`), 55 `dev/requirements//cases/*.png` (from `npm run refresh:ui`), and 56 `dev/requirements/extractor/generic-coverage/generic-coverage.baseline.GENERATED.json` 57 + `generic-coverage.GENERATED.md` (from the generic-coverage test). The 58 inline gallery in `dev/requirements/requirements.md` is part-authored prose — 59 **not** on the `ours` driver; reconcile via `npm run regen` + the gallery 60 drift gate. If `regen` reports a coverage regression, that's the real gate 61 firing — review it, don't paper over it. 62 - **Keep divergence small**: when syncing a branch to `origin/main` (by rebase), 63 **run `npm run regen`** as part of the sync, so the branch carries 64 freshly-generated artifacts, not just the latest sources. 65 - **Whenever a change regenerates the UI gallery** (via `npm run refresh:ui`), 66 link the branch's copy in the chat in the same turn you commit it — 67 `https://github.com///blob//dev/requirements/requirements.md` 68 — for one-page review. 69 70 ## Owner commands 71 72 - **"bump version"** = cut a release **end to end** — bump, merge, and wait for 73 the published artifact. The bump mechanics are the canon `bump-version` 74 skill's; honor an explicit target ("bump version to 1.4.0") or level ("bump 75 patch" / "bump major") when given. Open the PR, 76 get CI green, squash-merge with `(#N)` — 77 saying "bump version" is itself the merge authorization for **this** 78 deterministic bump PR only. The merge triggers **Release: Create Package**; 79 do **not** report done until the `vX.Y.Z` GitHub Release with its refreshed 80 `google-calendar-event-creator.zip` asset is published — poll via the GitHub 81 MCP tools on the merge-and-ci skill's back-off. 82 - **"learned lessons"** = run the canon lessons-learned pass over the current 83 conversation on **the strongest model available**. Capture routing: see below. 84 85 ## Testing invariants 86 87 - **Integration cases are the reviewed contract** — a person reads 88 `dev/requirements/extractor/expected/`; nobody reviews the unit tests. Every 89 required change or bugfix gets a case (one real, focused page per distinct 90 behavior; keep cases minimal). Unit tests under `extension-test/` are a 91 supplementary safety net for page-independent logic. 92 - **`extension-test/` mirrors `extension/`'s tree, one test per source file** 93 (`extension//.js` → `extension-test//.test.js`). 94 Deliberate departures: `extension-test/integration/` for 95 whole-extension/interaction tests; no mirror for `custom/*` sources or 96 data/markup files (covered by live cases / snapshots / drift guards); 97 `extension-test/harness.js` is shared infra (not a test) and stays at the 98 root. 99 - **The pinned `REFERENCE_NOW`** (`dev/requirements/shared/reference-time.js`, 100 currently 2026-06-01) **is the floor of the cases' dates**: author a 101 neutral/upcoming case **on or after it** so it's pill-free; use a past date or 102 a future year only when the case is *pinning* a pill. 103 104 ## Codebase gotchas 105 106 Project-wide footguns only. Portable rules these instantiate live in the canon 107 packs/skills. 108 109 - **`declarativeContent`/`UrlFilter` host-match verification is CI-only** — the 110 real URL→icon match runs inside Chrome, exercised here only by the CI-only 111 real-Chrome test (`dev/requirements/heavy/extension-load.chrome.test.js`). 112 - **CDP-introspecting the MV3 worker hits the portable traps** (canon): here 113 they bit `declarativeContent…getRules` (hung until job timeout), which is why 114 the worker publishes `globalThis.iconRulesReady` for the test to poll. 115 - **The jsdom-vs-Chrome DOM traps bit this repo directly** (canon): #130/#137 116 drove the **production** remedy the canon (framed for tests) leaves out — 117 strip `noscript`/`script`/`style` from a clone before reading any element's 118 user-facing text (the generic extractor's footer-address reader does this, #675). 119 - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it** — the parser 120 auto-closes the `

` and the content lands as its `nextElementSibling`; a 121 `.foo p` selector reads `""` with no error. Bit tel-aviv's description blocks 122 (#602) — read the sibling, not the tag. 123 - **The augment-not-replace + reset-per-load rule lands on `GCal` here** 124 (canon): `registry.js` resets `GCal.sources` on load and is pinned **first** 125 in the load order so it runs before any source pushes (#48, #189). 126 - **`clean()` collapses all whitespace including newlines — single-line fields 127 only.** A description run through it loses every line break (#131, #140, 128 #141); multi-line text goes through the block helpers (`blockText` / 129 `normalizeBlock` / `htmlToText`). Line-break handling is generic, never a 130 per-source choice. 131 - **A supported/registered host is necessary but not sufficient for "an 132 event"** — gating on `Boolean(site)` surfaced phantom events on home pages 133 (#133); a real event requires actual data (JSON-LD or a parsed date), never a 134 mere host match. 135 136 ## Workflow-failure classification 137 138 **Mind the one gap `gha/scheduled-failure-escalation` can't see:** it only 139 inspects workflows carrying a `schedule:`, so a workflow that is unattended by 140 some *other* trigger — `workflow_run`, `repository_dispatch` — needs its failure 141 job wired by hand. 142 The `Release` stub (`chrome-extension-release.yml`) is exactly that shape; its 143 reporters live in the vendored create-package/publish/daily workflows it calls. 144 145 ## Extractor pipeline 146 147 Standing rules for the extractor-automation domain — the two gcec pack 148 [`tasks/`](tasks/): **create-extractor** (an `extractor-request` issue → a PR 149 adding site support, and the sweep that records a committed `.url`'s missing 150 cached page) and the weekly **generic-extractor-improvements** (read a spec only when working 151 on that pipeline). Adding or refreshing a cached live case by hand is the 152 [testing-guide](skills/testing-guide/SKILL.md) skill. 153 154 - **All page fetching goes through [`scraperapi.mjs`](tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs), from a 155 task's preprocessing worker and nowhere else.** A rendered fetch through 156 ScraperAPI's residential proxy (`render=true`, so a single-page app records 157 post-render HTML with real data). Bot-blocking from CI/sandbox IPs is the 158 portable rule maintained in the canon; here the escape hatch is the 159 `SCRAPER_API_KEY` **GitHub Actions secret**, named in both tasks' 160 `required_secrets` — never a local fetch (this sandbox is bot-blocked), and 161 never an agent session. ScraperAPI is the whole fetching surface — swap the 162 vendor in that one module if it underperforms. The aid for a flaky SPA render is 163 the **`Wait-for selector`** a source request can carry 164 (`extension/events-popup/derive-wait-selector.js`, a source-request tool, NOT an 165 event extractor, #603), passed through as `wait_for_selector`. 166 - **Facebook can't be a cached live case** — a hard HTTP 400 even through the 167 proxy, so its extraction stays unit-tests-only 168 (`extension-test/event-extractors/extraction.test.js`). 169 - **A scratch script that needs a project dependency (e.g. `jsdom`) can't live 170 in the harness's external scratchpad** — Node's module resolution walks up 171 from the script's own directory, which never reaches this repo's 172 `node_modules`. `generic-extractor-improvements`' habitual "fetch a page, 173 then jsdom-inspect it" throwaway scripts need to live inside the repo (a 174 gitignored scratch dir, cleaned up before committing) instead (#866). 175 - **Rendered output isn't deterministic.** A re-record can legitimately shift a 176 live case's `expected` — treat such drift like a site-markup change, and prefer 177 extracting JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions. 178 - **An ambiguous numeric slash date is read by the page's declared locale, 179 centrally — never per-source, never guessed.** `"05/07/2026"` (both parts ≤ 12) 180 reads month-first by default (V8's US convention) and flips day-first only on a 181 *positive* non-US signal — an explicit non-US region in `` / 182 `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` (region unknown) stays 183 month-first rather than guess. Resolution lives in `helpers/dates.js` 184 (`parseDateFromText` / `normalizeDateValue` take a `dayFirst` flag, threaded 185 from `generic-extractor.js`'s `pageUsesDayFirstDates`), mirroring 186 `derive-timezone.js`'s locale read; unambiguous dates (a part > 12) and the 187 `.` / `-` separators are always day-first regardless (#686). 188 - **An unrecordable page is a dead end, not a failed run.** When a fetch can't 189 produce a page (bot wall, dead URL, empty render), create-extractor's 190 preprocessing labels the request `needs-human` with the reason 191 and exits **0** — a task failure would converge to a `needs-human` dispatch 192 issue as well, duplicating the signal and implying the pipeline broke when it 193 correctly declined. Same for the pending-page sweep: the pages that did record still land. 194 - **The generic-coverage gate is a high-watermark over a changing case set.** A 195 removed/renamed case the watermark still lists makes it stale: the local refresh re-anchors it 196 (commit that); in CI it's an error to fix. *Caveat:* never commit a re-anchored 197 baseline while the gate is red — a regression bundled with a case-set change can 198 be re-anchored over. Detailed mechanics self-document in the gate's own headers 199 (`dev/requirements/extractor/generic-coverage/generic-coverage.js` / `.test.js`). 200 - **To see what the core generic extractor gets ON ITS OWN** on any cached page — 201 even a supported host — load the files, set `GCal.sources = []`, then call 202 `GCal.extract()`: the documented way to strip every per-site override and see 203 the bare base through the same norm/sort the popup uses. (`GCal.extract()` 204 alone no longer answers this: the generic extractor is the base layer of every 205 extraction now, so on a supported host its output already carries the site's 206 overrides.) Most start/end *differences* vs a dedicated source are just its 207 hardcoded `ctz` localizing to floating time (same instant), not extraction 208 bugs; the real gaps are fields it can't know generically (durations, 209 site-specific descriptions, and — where the page doesn't declare corroborating 210 hints, see `helpers/derive-timezone.js` — `ctz`). This is the comparison the 211 generic-coverage gate automates — and a case where it shows NO gap is a 212 candidate for deleting the per-site source and listing the host in 213 `supportedDomains`). 214 215 ## Architecture rules of the road 216 217 Whenever we agree on a new or changed top-level architectural guideline, update 218 this section as part of the same change (the design doc itself is 219 `dev/procedures/highLevelDesign.md`): 220 221 - **`extension/event-extractors/custom/` is the extensibility point — one file 222 per site, and nothing else.** The rest of `event-extractors/` is the pipeline 223 itself: the registry, the orchestrator, the shared helpers, and the one core 224 generic extractor (`generic-extractor.js`), which is a different kind of thing 225 from a per-site file. 226 - **The core generic extractor is the base layer of every extraction** — it runs 227 on every page, and a per-site source is only a layer of *overrides* merged over 228 it, stating the fields it gets better. A source never re-reads what the page 229 already says about itself, and the generic extractor may never know about a 230 specific site. 231 - **Being supported is DECLARED, never derived from the extractors.** 232 `supportedDomains` in `extension/host-lists.json` is the one list of hosts 233 we claim, read directly by the toolbar worker and the popup. Never add a second 234 list, and never register a placeholder source just to make a host count as 235 supported. The only guarded direction is that every per-site source's host 236 appears in the list. 237 - **A site we fully support gets no extractor file when there is nothing to 238 override.** It stays listed in `supportedDomains` and stays fully supported — 239 green icon, no correction prompt — with no file at all. When a 240 `custom/.js` shrinks to nothing, just delete it; when such a site starts 241 needing a fix the generic extractor can't make site-agnostically, add the file 242 back. Never keep a file whose only content is a restatement of the generic 243 base, and never annotate one as "nothing to add". 244 - Adding support for a new host is the most common change — the architecture 245 must keep it a single-file change: a host added to `supportedDomains`, plus — 246 only when the generic extractor gets that site wrong — one self-contained new 247 `extension/event-extractors/custom/.js` and a regenerated load list, 248 touching nothing else and assuming nothing about other extractors. 249 250 ## Capture policy — lessons land in the local packs 251 252 Route each lesson to its section here: extractor-automation to the "Extractor 253 pipeline" section, everything else to the fitting section. 254
